claim.why_it_matters: A space was inserted into the PICTURE character-string. In COBOL a space terminates the PICTURE character-string, so the transcribed line is not the same source: it reads as PICTURE '$$$,$$$.' followed by a stray '99.' rather than the floating-dollar edited item with two decimal places the example (a packed-decimal print method) is illustrating. Verified by cropping and zooming the 300dpi render: the printed glyphs are contiguous, with no space between '.' and '99'.

verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed on both sides, and the refutation attempts all fail. (1) MARKDOWN SIDE: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 46353 literally reads '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$. 99.' -- the space is in the canonical transcription, not an artifact of the workunit extractor. It is not reflow or wrapping: the line sits inside a fenced code block with the rest of the example intact, so there is no adjacent line the '99' could have migrated from. (2) PDF SIDE: rendered page 1151 at 300dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v1151/spec_p1151.png, printed folio 1121) and cropped/upscaled the line 3x. The printed text is '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$.99.' with no gap. (3) PIXEL PROOF, not eyeballing: the example is set in a monospace face. Measuring glyph-ink column runs, the pitch is 26.9 px (glyph '0' at x=339, '1' at x=365; the leading '01' + two spaces + 'O' of 'Out-p' at x=443 = 339 + 4*26 confirms the pitch against a KNOWN pair of spaces). The eleven glyphs of the picture string occupy eleven CONSECUTIVE cells: $ 712, $ 739, $ 766, ',' 794, $ 819, $ 846, $ 873, '.' 905, 9 927, 9 954, '.' 985 -- every one within +/-1 px of its predicted cell origin except the two narrow period glyphs, which sit +5/+4 px in from the cell edge exactly as a centered period must. The largest inter-glyph advance anywhere in that run is 32 px, i.e. one cell; a space would require ~54 px, and would push the first '9' to x~954 and the trailing '.' to x~1008. It does not. There is no blank cell between '.' and '99'. (4) The difference is not formatting and does change meaning: it corrupts the source text of the example. Severity 'cosmetic' is nonetheless fair -- this is a non-normative EXAMPLE in the INVOKE/method discussion, so no normative rule the compiler must implement is affected. Sibling lines on the page were spot-checked and transcribe correctly ('pic ZZZ,ZZZ,ZZZ.', 'pic s9(5)v99 packed-decimal.', 'pic x(20).', 'pic 9(4).'), so this is an isolated character-level OCR insertion, not a systematic one.
verdict.corrected_description: Confirmed real, with one correction to the claim's COBOL analysis. The PDF prints '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$.99.'; specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 46353 transcribes it as '01  Out-p pic $$$,$$$. 99.' with a spurious space between the decimal point and '99'. The claim's consequence is directionally right but states the resulting PICTURE slightly wrong: it says the line would read as PICTURE '$$$,$$$.' (period included) plus a stray '99.'. In fact a period followed by a space is a separator period, so the corrupted line parses as PICTURE '$$$,$$$' -- WITHOUT the decimal point -- terminating the data description entry there, leaving '99.' as an orphan clause. The corruption is therefore slightly worse than described: it drops the decimal point as well as the two decimal digit positions, turning the floating-dollar item with two decimal places (the whole point of an example whose linkage item is 'pic s9(5)v99 packed-decimal') into an integer-only floating-dollar item, and leaves invalid residue behind. Correct fix: delete the space, restoring 'pic $$$,$$$.99.'.
